claim_en: Belle's near-threshold enhancement in e⁺e⁻ → Λc⁺Λ̄c⁻ (M ≈ 4634 MeV, PRL 101 (2008) 172001) is not seen by BESIII at twelve energies from 4.61 to 4.95 GeV (PRL 131 (2023) 191901).
2025 was the LHC's record proton year: ATLAS and CMS each received 125.4 fb⁻¹, 1.5 fb⁻¹ more than the 2024 record and achieved in about 14 fewer days; LHCb received 12.6 fb⁻¹.

Using laser-cooled beryllium ions to cool positrons below 10 K, ALPHA trapped more than 15,000 antihydrogen atoms in under 7 hours. CERN describes this as an eightfold increase in the production rate. Before, accumulating 16,000 atoms took about 10 weeks, and Swansea says previous methods 'took 24 hours to trap just 2,000 atoms'. Published in Nature Communications, November 2025.

On 27 May 2026 ALPHA reported in Nature that the ground-state hyperfine splitting of antihydrogen (the antimatter version of hydrogen's famous 21-cm radio line) matches hydrogen's to within 4 parts per million, 100 times more precise than its 2017 result of 400 ppm.

CERN's Antimatter Factory (AD + ELENA), which CERN calls 'a unique machine', delivers about 400 million antiprotons per hour to experiments. All the antiprotons it would produce running non-stop for a whole year would amount to about 500 J, enough to light a 100 W bulb for five seconds. ELENA slows antiprotons from 5.3 MeV to 0.1 MeV (factor 50). Five experiments use the AD/ELENA (AEgIS, ALPHA, ASACUSA, BASE, GBAR), and the antimatter page also lists PUMA.
In July 2025 the BASE collaboration published in Nature the first antimatter qubit, a single antiproton whose spin was made to oscillate coherently between two quantum states for about 50 seconds.

On 24 March 2026 the BASE team carried 92 antiprotons in a ~1,000 kg portable superconducting Penning trap (BASE-STEP) by truck across CERN's main site, about 30 minutes at up to 42 km/h, and kept the experiment running afterwards, a world first.

In 2026 CERN's 25 Member States contribute 1,232,149,900 CHF in total; Germany is the largest contributor (20.44%, 251.9 MCHF), followed by the UK (15.07%, 185.7 MCHF) and France (12.96%, 159.7 MCHF); Associate Member States add 44.5 MCHF and Cyprus (pre-stage) 1.15 MCHF.
British particle physicist Mark Thomson became CERN Director-General on 1 January 2026 for a five-year mandate, succeeding Fabiola Gianotti; the CERN Council selected him on 6 November 2024.

On 22 May 2026, at its 227th session in Budapest, the CERN Council adopted the 2026 update of the European Strategy for Particle Physics, which names the FCC-ee as the preferred next flagship collider, a descoped FCC-ee (about 15% cheaper) as the preferred alternative, completion of the HL-LHC as the top priority, and asks management to make a Council decision on FCC-ee possible by 2028.

In December 2025 CERN passed one exabyte (one million terabytes) of stored LHC experimental data, kept mostly on about 60,000 magnetic tapes, and CERN says this is only about 10% of what it will need to store and process over the next 10 years.

At a dedicated session on 6–7 November 2025 the CERN Council concluded that the FCC Feasibility Study 'provides the basis for the FCC studies to continue' and reaffirmed its aim to reach a final decision on the FCC 'possibly in 2028'.

The FCC Feasibility Study, released on 31 March 2025, proposes a 90.7 km ring at an average depth of about 200 m with 8 surface sites and 4 experiments, whose first stage (the FCC-ee electron–positron collider) would cost about 15 billion CHF spread over roughly 12–15 years from the early 2030s.
In 1995 the PS210 experiment at CERN's LEAR ring made the first antihydrogen atoms ever (about 9 atoms), which flew at nearly the speed of light and annihilated almost immediately.

The CERN Convention was signed in Paris on 1 July 1953 by 12 founding states (Belgium, Denmark, France, West Germany, Greece, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, UK, Yugoslavia), and CERN officially came into being on 29 September 1954; the acronym comes from the provisional 'Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire' (coined Feb 1952).

LHC experiments have discovered more than 85 new hadrons, including a doubly charmed baryon Ξcc (two charm quarks and a down quark, about four times heavier than a proton) that LHCb announced on 17 March 2026 at 7σ, the first new particle seen with its upgraded Run 3 detector.

On 4 July 2012 ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of the Higgs boson at CERN, and on 8 October 2013 François Englert and Peter Higgs received the Nobel Prize in Physics, with a citation that explicitly names the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's LHC.

ALICE measured that near-miss lead–lead collisions turn lead into gold. During Run 2 (2015–2018) about 86 billion gold nuclei were created at the four major LHC experiments, just 29 picograms (2.9×10⁻¹¹ g) in total. The LHC currently (Run 3) produces gold at a maximum of about 89,000 nuclei per second from Pb–Pb collisions at the ALICE collision point. The gold exists for just a tiny fraction of a second.
The LHC's superconducting magnets operate at 1.9 K (−271.3 °C), colder than outer space (2.7 K), and 23 km of the 27 km ring is cooled with superfluid helium.
Each LHC beam holds about 2,500 bunches of roughly 1.6×10¹¹ protons, 25 ns apart, producing about 1.5 billion proton collisions per second inside ATLAS and CMS.
In Run 3 (2022–2026) each LHC proton beam carried 6.8 TeV, giving record 13.6 TeV collisions; lead ions collided at 5.36 TeV per nucleon pair.
The LHC contains 9,593 magnets, including 1,232 main dipoles, each 15 m long, and 392 main quadrupoles 5–7 m long.
The LHC uses roughly 600 GWh of electricity per year, peaking at 695 GWh in 2024, and CERN has committed to keep its total electricity use at or below 1.5 TWh per year by 2030.

The LHC is a 26,659 m ring about 100 m underground. CERN's construction (materials) cost was 4,332 MCHF: 3,756 MCHF for the LHC machine and areas (including R&D, injectors and tests), 493 MCHF as CERN's share of detectors and detector areas, and 83 MCHF as CERN's share of computing. CERN gives the total cost of all LHC detectors as about 1,500 MCHF, most of it paid by the collaborating institutes.

At 6.8 TeV an LHC proton has γ ≈ 7,247 and 1−β ≈ 9.5×10⁻⁹, so v ≈ 99.99999905% of c, about 2.85 m/s slower than light. It goes round the 26.659 km ring 11,245 times per second, and on each lap it falls behind a light signal by about 0.25 mm, not 0.25 nm.
The energy stored in an LHC beam reached 490 MJ during Run 3 and will rise to up to 710 MJ in the HL-LHC era, which is why a dedicated beam-dump system must absorb it safely.
The LHC beam pipes hold an ultra-high vacuum of about 10⁻¹³ bar, ten million million times lower than atmospheric pressure at sea level.
In early July 2025 the LHC collided oxygen nuclei for the first time (and also neon, plus proton–oxygen) to study quark–gluon plasma in small systems and cosmic-ray air showers.

Lithuania has been a CERN Associate Member State since 8 January 2018 (the first Baltic state to obtain that status), and its 2026 contribution to the CERN budget is 1,000,000 CHF; associate status lets Lithuanian nationals apply for CERN staff jobs and Lithuanian companies bid for CERN contracts.

In Long Shutdown 3 (July 2026 to 2030) CERN is removing and replacing about 1.2 km of LHC magnets and components for the High-Luminosity LHC, which is due to restart gradually from 2028, start physics in June 2030 and run until 2041 with up to 10 times the original design luminosity.

As of October 2026 CERN has 25 Member States and 11 Associate Member States (Brazil, Chile, Croatia, Cyprus [pre-stage], India, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Pakistan, Türkiye, Ukraine). Japan and the USA are observers with respect to the LHC (the USA also for the HL-LHC), and the EU and UNESCO are observers. JINR's observer status has been suspended since 25 March 2022. Russia's observer status was suspended on 8 March 2022, and CERN then ended all cooperation with Russia when its agreement expired on 30 November 2024 (Belarus on 27 June 2024).

Ireland became an Associate Member State on 22 October 2025 and Chile on 2 April 2026, which brought CERN to 25 Member States and 11 Associate Member States; Chilean institutes already take part in ATLAS, CMS and LHCb.
Estonia became CERN's 24th Member State on 30 August 2024 (the first Baltic country to become a full member) and Slovenia became the 25th Member State on 21 June 2025.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, announced on 6 October 2026 (the day before this research), went to Francis Halzen 'for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin'; IceCube is a CERN Recognized Experiment and CERN DG Mark Thomson congratulated him, but it is not a CERN experiment.

Since its first collisions the LHC delivered nearly 550 fb⁻¹, almost twice the original target of 300 fb⁻¹ and about 50 times the combined data of all earlier hadron colliders. In Run 3 alone, ATLAS and CMS each received about 4×10¹⁶ proton–proton collisions. ATLAS recorded 505 fb⁻¹ over its lifetime, 332 fb⁻¹ of it in Run 3.

CERN's Science Gateway outreach centre, designed by Renzo Piano, opened on 7–8 October 2023. It was funded entirely by about 100 million CHF of private donations (45 MCHF from the Stellantis Foundation), aims for up to 500,000 visitors a year and is carbon neutral thanks to almost 4,000 m² of solar panels.
CERN's first 500 PB of stored LHC data took about 12 years to collect; the second 500 PB, which brought it to one exabyte in December 2025, came in Run 3 alone (from 2022).
CERN itself employs about 2,500 staff members who design, build and operate the infrastructure, while the user community spans more than 110 nationalities and institutes in more than 70 countries.
CERN had 12,639 registered users (visiting scientists) in 2025, up from just 121 in 1970: 7,637 nationals of Member States, 1,171 of Associate Member States and 3,831 of non-member states.

The Worldwide LHC Computing Grid links over 170 sites in 42 countries with about 1.4 million CPU cores and 1.5 exabytes of storage, runs more than 2 million tasks per day, and CERN supplies about 20% of its resources (the CERN Data Centre alone runs ~10,000 servers with ~450,000 cores).
CMS alone has over 4 PB on the CERN Open Data portal: over 300 collision datasets and over 20 000 simulated datasets.

claim_en: CERN published the first CERN Open Hardware Licence in 2011 and version 2.0 in March 2020, in three variants: strongly reciprocal (S), weakly reciprocal (W) and permissive (P). The Open Source Initiative approved the CERN-OHL v2 family as OSI-certified licences on 15 January 2021.

When running, the LHC is the world's largest cryogenic system. Its main superconducting magnets (1,232 dipoles) operate at 1.9 K (-271.3 °C), colder than the 2.7 K of outer space, using about 120 tonnes of helium and cooling some 36,000 tonnes of cold mass. Since Long Shutdown 3 began on 29 June 2026 the LHC has been warmed back to room temperature for the HL-LHC upgrade.

Geant4, a toolkit that simulates the passage of particles through matter, was approved at CERN as R&D project RD44 in November 1994 and first released on 15 December 1998. By the end of 2023 its main reference paper had more than 16,000 citations, the most cited publication in particle and fields physics, nuclear physics, and nuclear science and technology.

Geant4 was first used for space by ESA in 1999. It identified why NASA's Chandra X-ray telescope (launched July 1999) was losing detection capability, since low-energy trapped protons were scattering off the mirrors onto the CCDs, and this allowed ESA to take countermeasures for XMM-Newton.
By September 2023 MedAustron had treated 2,000 patients with protons or carbon ions, with about 50 irradiations per day in three treatment rooms.

The Proton-Ion Medical Machine Study (PIMMS) was carried out at CERN in 1996-2000 under Phil Bryant as an open 'toolkit' design for a proton and carbon-ion cancer-therapy synchrotron. TERA adapted it for CNAO in Pavia, Italy, which treated its first patient in 2011, and it was also used for MedAustron in Wiener Neustadt, Austria, certified in December 2016, which treated its first patient a few days later.

In March 2020, during the COVID-19 lockdown, members of the LHCb VELO group led by CERN engineer Jan Buytaert designed the HEV (High Energy physics community Ventilator). The design reused particle-detector gas-control know-how and standard parts such as electro-valves, a 2-litre buffer, Arduino and Raspberry Pi.

Indico, an event-management platform adopted by CERN in 2004 and funded by CERN since, ran on about 300 servers in 52 countries for some 400,000 users as of February 2024 and managed about 145,000 events worldwide in 2023. Users include the United Nations.

CERN-MEDICIS, which produces medical radionuclides by mass separation, collected its first radionuclide in 2017. In April 2025 it restarted after a shutdown with a programme in which, following a positive CERN Council decision, MEDICIS-separated treatment radionuclides may be used in clinical research in hospitals for the first time. It builds on ISOLDE, which has produced about 1,300 different isotopes of 73 chemical elements.

On 12 July 2018 it was announced that New Zealand company MARS Bioimaging, linked to the Universities of Otago and Canterbury, had made the first 3D colour X-ray of a human using CERN's Medipix3 chip. The scanner was developed over a decade by father-and-son scientists Phil and Anthony Butler, under a licence agreement between CERN (on behalf of the Medipix3 collaboration) and MARS Bioimaging.

Townsend spent 8 years at CERN from 1970, then worked at the Geneva Cantonal Hospital from 1979 to 1993, where he saw the value of combining PET with CT. The Partial Ring Tomograph (PRT) PET prototype was developed at CERN in 1989-1990 and evaluated clinically at the Cantonal Hospital.

In early summer 1977 at CERN, Alan Jeavons' high-density avalanche chamber detector and David Townsend's reconstruction software produced the first PET image taken at CERN, of a mouse injected by CERN radiobiologist Marilena (Streit-)Bianchi. The results were presented at a conference in October 1977.

The combined PET/CT scanner was developed by former CERN physicist David Townsend (University of Pittsburgh) and Ronald Nutt (CTI PET Systems), with NCI funding from 1995. The first clinical PET/CT images were shown in 1998, TIME named PET/CT 'Medical Invention of the Year' in December 2000, and the first commercial Siemens Biograph PET/CT was installed in Pittsburgh by mid-2001.
ROOT, an object-oriented C++ framework 'born at CERN' for storing and analysing petabytes of data, started in January 1995. René Brun was one of the project founders, with Fons Rademakers.

Ultra-high-vacuum technology developed at CERN (getter strips for LEP, then thin-film NEG getter coatings developed for the LHC) was turned by CERN vacuum physicist Cristoforo Benvenuti into high-temperature solar thermal panels made by spin-off SRB Energy (founded 2005 with Spain's Grupo Segura). In 2012 about 300 panels covering 1,200 m² were contracted for Geneva Airport's main terminal roof.

Orion on Artemis I (uncrewed, 2022) carried NASA's Timepix-based HERA monitor, and its data, published in 2024, showed dose equivalents about 30% lower than earlier literature values. Artemis II, which launched at 00:35 CEST on 2 April 2026 (evening of 1 April in Florida), carried six CERN-developed Timepix chips in HERA to monitor the radiation dose of the four astronauts.

NASA began testing CERN-derived Timepix detectors on the ISS in 2012. A battery-powered version flew on Orion EFT-1 in 2014 and 'provided the first radiation belt data from beyond low-Earth orbit within a human-rated space vehicle since the Apollo missions'.

Czech start-up InsightART used CERN's Timepix photon-counting chips in its RToo X-ray scanner to map the elemental composition of the paint in a 'Madonna and Child' attributed to Raphael. Over three days it took 11 high-resolution images at different X-ray energies, which helped experts in authenticating the painting.

CERN's touchscreen used capacitors made of copper lines etched on glass, 'fine enough (80 μm) and sufficiently far apart (80 μm) to be invisible'. The first prototype used a thin layer of copper or gold evaporated onto a flexible, transparent Mylar sheet.

The first finger-driven touchscreen was described in 1965 by E.A. (Eric) Johnson of the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, UK, in 'Touch Display - A novel input/output device for computers' (Electronics Letters 1(8):219-220). It used capacitive sensing and was programmed for air-traffic-control tasks.

When the SPS started in 1976 its control room was fully equipped with touch screens, 'apparently the first application of the capacitative touch screen in the world'. By 1977 the screen was commercially available and sold to users inside CERN and to other institutes and companies. Its use then spread to JET and the Rutherford Laboratory (UK), KEK, Mitsubishi and TOYO (Japan), Rigshospitalet (Denmark) and the Hahn-Meitner Institute (Germany). Some CERN screens ran until the CERN Control Centre took over in 2006, a 30-year lifetime.

On 11 March 1972 CERN engineer Bent Stumpe, at the request of Frank Beck (later head of SPS Central Controls), proposed in a handwritten note a capacitive touch screen with a fixed number of programmable buttons on a display to control CERN's new Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS). Beck and Stumpe described it in a 1973 CERN report.

White Rabbit, an open-source timing technology developed at CERN and first used in 2012, synchronises thousands of nodes over fibre Ethernet with sub-nanosecond accuracy and picosecond precision. In 2020 its concepts were incorporated into the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol standard (IEEE 1588-2019) as the High Accuracy profile.

The White Rabbit Collaboration, launched at CERN in March 2024, grew from 8 founding partners to 18 members in a year. Four members come from finance: Deutsche Börse uses WR to monitor that its trading system stays fair and to offer a precision timestamp service; Quincy Data provides a WR timing service; Jump Trading is exploring WR; and Liquid-Markets Solutions built a WR network card.

The Worldwide LHC Computing Grid (WLCG) combines about 1.4 million computer cores and 1.5 exabytes of storage from over 170 sites in 42 countries. It runs over 2 million tasks per day for more than 12,000 physicists, and global transfer rates exceeded 260 GB/s at the end of LHC Long Shutdown 2.

The formal proposal 'WorldWideWeb: Proposal for a HyperText Project' (T. Berners-Lee/CN, R. Cailliau/ECP) is dated 12 November 1990. Phase 1 had a target of '3 months from start' and Phase 2 '6 months from start' ('phase two a further 3 months'), so the plan totalled about 6 months, not 9. It asked for 4 software engineers and a programmer. Phase 1 browsers were for dumb terminals, VT220, Macintosh and NeXT; Phase 2 added VM/XA and an X-window browser/editor.

By Christmas 1990 the first browser/editor, website and server were live at CERN (CERN Web@30 timeline: 'December 1990'). The exact date of 20 December 1990 appears only in secondary sources such as Wikipedia.

The first website defined the project as 'a wide-area hypermedia information retrieval initiative aiming to give universal access to a large universe of documents'. In 2013 CERN restored this first website at info.cern.ch, where it can still be browsed, including through a line-mode browser simulator.

By late 1993 there were over 500 known web servers. By the end of 1994 the web had 10,000 servers, 2,000 of them commercial, and 10 million users. In 1994 Berners-Lee left CERN for MIT and founded the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).

By the end of 1990 Berners-Lee had the first web server and browser running at CERN on a NeXT computer that carried the handwritten label 'This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!'. The first website address was info.cern.ch.

Nicola Pellow wrote the 'line-mode' browser during her student placement at CERN, so the web could be used from any simple terminal. In 1991 Berners-Lee released the WWW software and in August 1991 announced it on Internet newsgroups.

In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee at CERN wrote 'Information Management: A Proposal'. Its opening line frames the web as an answer to a CERN and LHC-era problem: 'Many of the discussions of the future at CERN and the LHC era end with the question - Yes, but how will we ever keep track of such a large project?'

On 30 April 1993 CERN Directors Walter Hoogland (Research) and Helmut Weber (Administration) signed an internal 'to whom it may concern' document releasing the WWW software into the public domain: 'CERN relinquishes all intellectual property rights to this code, both source and binary form, and permission is granted for anyone to use, duplicate, modify and redistribute it.' In 1994 the next version came out under an open-source licence with CERN keeping copyright, announced by François Flückiger on 15 November 1994.

Berners-Lee's manager Mike Sendall called the proposal 'vague, but exciting'; the famous handwritten 'Vague but exciting...' is on the cover of the March 1989 proposal. In September 1990 Sendall approved buying a NeXT cube and allowed Berners-Lee to go ahead and write a global hypertext system.
Netcraft's July 2026 Web Server Survey found 1,494,915,628 sites across 305,348,459 domains on 14,772,048 web-facing computers.

Tim Berners-Lee received the 2016 ACM A.M. Turing Award 'for inventing the World Wide Web, the first web browser, and the fundamental protocols and algorithms allowing the Web to scale', and was knighted in the 2004 New Year Honours.
ITU estimates that about 6 billion people, 74% of the world's population, used the Internet in 2025, while 2.2 billion remain offline.

Zenodo, CERN's free open-research repository built with OpenAIRE for the European Commission's open-data policy and running on CERN's open-source InvenioRDM, launched in May 2013. By its 10th anniversary in May 2023 it served about 300,000 researchers from 7,500+ organisations in 153 countries.

claim_en: A 2003 CERN supplier survey covering 629 technology-intensive suppliers and EUR 768 million of procurement found that 38% developed new products, 44% acquired significant technological learning, 60% gained new customers and 13% created new R&D teams. Extrapolated, that is about 500 new products and about 1,900 new customers outside high-energy physics.

ADVACAM, a Prague company founded in 2013 that commercialises CERN Medipix/Timepix photon-counting technology, builds Timepix modules used in space (e.g. the VZLUSAT-1 X-ray telescope, 2017) and supplies Timepix modules for NASA's Artemis missions.

In the 2025 CERN Alumni Network survey, 95% of 982 respondents said CERN had helped their careers. About three-quarters of CERN alumni move into industry, and they report an average wage premium of 4%.

Artemis II launched at 00:35 CEST on 2 April 2026, the first crewed journey to the Moon since 1972. It carried six CERN-designed Timepix chips in NASA's HERA system to measure radiation inside Orion, with chip modules supplied by Czech CERN partner ADVACAM.

CERN's CHARM facility has run more than 300 system-level radiation tests for industry and research in the past decade, 172 of them in 2024. The VESPER set-up at CERN's CLEAR accelerator is the only facility on Earth able to reproduce Jupiter's extreme electron radiation environment, which was used for ESA's JUICE mission.
By July 2026 Italy's CNAO in Pavia had treated more than 6,200 patients with hadron therapy. It is one of only 8 'dual-particle' centres in the world offering both protons and carbon ions.
In 2025, 8 startups joined CERN Venture Connect, whose partner network numbered 60 organisations in 18 countries. CVC startups raised CHF 5.6 million (over EUR 5 million) during the year.
CERN Venture Connect gives startups fast-track licences to CERN technologies on a novel deal structure: a 2% royalty that becomes payable only once the startup reaches CHF 1 million in sales.

The Global Innovation Index 2026 (WIPO, released 29 September 2026) features CERN Venture Connect in its special-theme chapter. CVC was launched in 2023 and currently works with 21 startups, offers 9 CERN technologies and has more than 50 partners.

Florio, Forte and Sirtori (Technological Forecasting and Social Change 112, 2016) estimated, conservatively, a ~90% probability that the LHC's benefits exceed its costs, with an expected NPV of about EUR 2.9 billion (1993 to the then-planned decommissioning in 2025). The estimate does not count 'the unpredictable applications of scientific discovery'. It does include taxpayers' willingness to pay for LHC knowledge as a pure public good.

CERN's Proton-Ion Medical Machine Study (PIMMS, 1996-2000), carried out with TERA, MedAustron and Onkologie-2000, laid the groundwork for Italy's CNAO and Austria's MedAustron. Together the two centres have treated nearly 9,000 patients with rare and hard-to-treat cancers since opening in 2011 and 2016.

A new CERN socio-economic analysis of the High-Luminosity LHC, published 23 September 2026, finds that returns are expected to be nearly twice the investment, with 94% of 50,000 Monte Carlo simulations giving a positive net result. Training of people accounts for 40.3% of the benefits and industrial suppliers plus free software for 37.7%.
CERN's Industrial Liaison Officer for Lithuania is Ms Aušrinė Krištopaitytė of Innovation Agency Lithuania (Vilnius). The 'Who to contact in your country' page lists ILOs for 35 countries.

In 2025 CERN signed 89 knowledge-transfer contracts: 32 collaborative R&D, 28 licences, 15 service/consultancy, 8 CERN Venture Connect startup agreements, 3 contract research, 2 co-ownership and 1 other. 63 of the partners were companies.

For 1 March 2025 to 28 February 2026, Lithuania (an associate member contributing CHF 1.0 million, 0.08% of CERN's 2025 budget) was classed as 'poorly balanced' for industrial return on supply contracts, meaning Lithuanian firms won a smaller share of CERN supply contracts than Lithuania's budget share. CERN's procurement rules contain mechanisms, such as price alignment and limited tendering, to improve returns to poorly balanced states.

In March 2026 (DOTmed report dated 24 March 2026), New Zealand company MARS Bioimaging received US FDA 510(k) clearance for its portable photon-counting CT 'Extremity Scanner System' for upper-extremity imaging. The system is built on CERN's Medipix3 chip under a licence agreement between CERN (on behalf of the Medipix3 Collaboration) and MARS Bioimaging.

MARS Bioimaging CTO Anthony Butler, whose father had worked at CERN, said after the FDA clearance: 'Twenty years later, with the support of the Medipix Collaboration, we are starting to have a significant impact.'

MedAustron in Wiener Neustadt, whose accelerator design is based on PIMMS and was developed with CERN, treated about 550 patients in 2025. It plans to add two treatment rooms to reach about 1,000 patients a year.

Medipix/Timepix read-out chips, developed by four Medipix Collaborations of about 40 institutes since the 1990s, now have 30 active commercial licences. These have earned more than CHF 5 million in royalties, supported an estimated CHF 100 million or more of industry revenue, and underpin 73 patents by companies such as Philips, ASML and Siemens. 40% of all licences were signed in the last three years.

CERN openlab, a public-private R&D partnership started in 2001 and now in its eighth three-year phase (from 2024), works with companies including Oracle, Siemens, NVIDIA, Intel, Pasqal and Johnson & Johnson.

Econometric analysis of CERN suppliers with first orders between 1995 and 2008 shows that becoming a CERN industrial partner raises the likelihood of filing a first patent and the number of patent applications, but only after a 5 to 8 year 'gestation lag'.

In 1977 CERN physicists David Townsend and Alan Jeavons produced one of the first PET images, of a mouse, using a high-density avalanche chamber detector and reconstruction software. CERN states that 'PET was not invented at CERN' but that this work contributed significantly to its development. Townsend later co-developed the combined PET/CT scanner in the US, and more than 1,000 PET/CT scanners were in use by 2005.

CERN spent about CHF 613 million on procurement in 2024. Price enquiries cover CHF 10,000-400,000, and any above CHF 50,000 are also sent to national Industrial Liaison Officers. Contracts above CHF 400,000 go through a published market survey followed by an invitation to tender for qualified firms, and suppliers must register in CERN's Suppliers Portal.

Proton (originally ProtonMail), the encrypted e-mail and privacy company, was founded in Geneva in 2014 by scientists who met at CERN, including Andy Yen. More than 300 CERN people beta-tested it, and its launch crowdfunding drew over 10,000 backers and more than USD 500,000. Its main shareholder is now the non-profit Proton Foundation.
IDC counted 1.26 billion smartphones shipped worldwide in 2025, each with a touch screen. This gives the scale of the touch-interface industry that CERN's early work is part of.

An independent study by Technopolis and CSIL, published by CERN in 2026, found that CERN has signed more than 700 knowledge-transfer contracts since 2011, including licences and collaborative R&D agreements.
In CERN's 2024 procurement survey, 54% of suppliers reported entering new markets as a direct result of working with CERN, and 70% said they developed advanced expertise.

CERN, Lausanne's CHUV hospital and THERYQ (ALCEN group) are building FLASHDEEP, a compact linear accelerator based on CERN's CLIC technology. It is designed to deliver 100-200 MeV electron FLASH radiotherapy in under 100 ms to tumours up to 20 cm deep. The project received EUR 38 million from France 2030, installation at Gustave Roussy is planned for late 2026, and first trials are planned for 2027.
Market research firm SNS Insider valued the global touch-screen display market at USD 76.36 billion in 2023 and forecasts USD 194.44 billion by 2032.

CERN engineer Bent Stumpe proposed a capacitive touch screen in a handwritten note dated 11 March 1972, and with Frank Beck built transparent capacitive touch screens for the SPS control room, in use from 1973. Three main consoles each had a 16-button touch screen, and Stumpe said they stayed in operation for more than 20 years.

Deutsche Börse deployed White Rabbit for sub-nanosecond timestamping across all participant cross-connects in its co-location: more than 500 ports, 60 devices and 4 data-centre modules. It now offers White Rabbit time services to trading participants.

Czech research network CESNET joined CERN's White Rabbit Collaboration (announced July 2026) as its first Czech member. According to TechTimes, CESNET has deployed White Rabbit timing over about 2,500 km of fibre alongside live 400 Gbps data traffic on the GÉANT pan-European research backbone.

On 16 July 2026, India's Union Minister Pralhad Joshi commissioned a White Rabbit-based Indian Standard Time Dissemination DEMONSTRATION Network at the Regional Reference Standard Laboratory (RRSL) in Bengaluru, developed by the Department of Consumer Affairs, CSIR-NPL and ISRO. Secure dissemination of IST between RRSL Bengaluru and NSE Chennai was verified with partners including SEBI, NSE and BSNL. The government says the project will 'reduce dependence on foreign timing sources'.

A WIFO study commissioned by CERN (December 2025) estimates that CERN procurement generates about CHF 680 million a year in direct, indirect and induced value added (1999-2024 average). Average annual procurement was about CHF 570 million, spread over 40,000 to 90,000 orders a year, and about 13% of the value added ends up outside CERN member states, mainly in China.

Zenodo, the open research repository built and run by CERN with the EU's OpenAIRE programme, held about 7.43 million public records on 7 October 2026. It serves more than 300,000 researchers in about 7,500 organisations.
In May 2026 CERN launched an internal Entrepreneurship Academy with a first cohort of 23 CERN personnel to train researchers to create spin-outs.

After the SCALE demonstrator (2022–2024), a 7 m flexible superconducting REBCO power line for hydrogen aircraft that ran at ±2 kA up to 63 K with cables of about 290 g/m, CERN and Airbus UpNext started SAMBA in 2025, due to finish by end 2026. Its lightweight HTS cables are meant for Airbus's Cryoprop demonstrator, a 2 MW-class superconducting electric propulsion system.

The EU's CERN-led ATTRACT programme closed in July 2025 after investing EUR 60 million of public funding in 170 early-stage detection and imaging R&D projects. It led to 8 start-ups and trained more than 1,300 young innovators, and the European Commission named it one of the top five projects contributing to the New European Innovation Agenda.

CAFEIN, CERN's federated-learning AI platform, was runner-up in the Digital Frontiers category of the Digital@UNGA Awards 2026. It lets hospitals train AI models together on patient data without sharing that data, and it runs projects in stroke (TRUSTroke, UMBRELLA) and clinical decision support (AIM-SAFE).

CERN's Innovation Programme on Environmental Applications (CIPEA) had more than 25 projects under way in Nov 2025, and more than 80% of its funding came from external industrial and academic partners. Examples include superconducting grid cables (SuperNode), superconducting cables for hydrogen aircraft (Airbus), fusion (Gauss Fusion, ENI, ITER), ocean-plastic detection from space (Edge SpAIce/hls4ml) and ink-free laser marking of food packaging (InPhocal).

From its launch in Oct 2023 to April 2026, CVC enrolled 18 companies, 7 of them (39%) founded by CERN alumni, and it had 150 venture leads by the end of March 2026. Its predecessor, the BIC incubation network (est. 2012), incubated 43 start-ups in 11 years across 10 national centres, an average of 3.9 per year, against about 6.5 per year for CVC in its first two years.

CVC's standard licence takes no equity. CERN charges a 2% royalty on revenue made with the licensed technology, nothing is due until the company reaches CHF 1 million in annual sales (investment rounds excluded), and the licence is 10 years, worldwide, non-exclusive and limited to one field of application.

CERN published the Technical Design Report for DEFT (Deep Electron FLASH Therapy), the accelerator behind the CHUV–CERN–THERYQ project. It produces 140 MeV electrons to treat tumours up to 25 cm deep and up to 20 cm across, delivering 20–30 Gy in under 0.1 s, using X-band RF technology from CERN's CLIC study.

Through the EU Edge SpAIce project (started 2024), CERN's open-source hls4ml tool is being adapted to run compressed neural networks on board satellites. The target platform is EnduroSat's Balkan-1 (launched 14 Jan 2025 on SpaceX Transporter-12), and the goal is to detect marine plastic litter from orbit. CERN showcased the technology at a UN Plastic Treaty (INC-5.2) side event at IdeaSquare on 8 Aug 2025.

CERN–ESA cooperation (bilateral agreement signed about ten years before the CERN Courier article of early 2025) produced CELESTA, CERN's first satellite (1 kg, 10 cm cube, launched July 2022). CELESTA flight-tested the SpaceRadMon radiation monitor, which was later adopted by ESA's Trisat and GENA-OT missions. CERN's VESPER set-up at the CLEAR facility (60–200 MeV electrons) is described by CERN as the only facility on Earth able to reproduce Jupiter's electron radiation environment for ground tests for ESA's JUICE mission. CHARM: 300+ system-level tests in a decade, 172 of them in 2024.

CERN won EU Horizon Europe funding for 13 new projects from calls announced in 2025, which CERN calls the highest number in a single year since at least 2007. CERN coordinates 5 of them: ATTRACT EXPAND (EUR 10M), EPITA (EUR 21M total), RADNEXT 2030 (EUR 12M total), PRISMAP+ (EUR 5M) and iRIS (EUR 5M). EPITA and RADNEXT 2030 received the maximum evaluation score of 15/15.

For the first time in CERN's history, private donors pledged money for a CERN flagship project: about EUR 860 million (USD 1 billion) towards the Future Circular Collider, from the Breakthrough Prize Foundation, the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Fund for Strategic Innovation, John Elkann and Xavier Niel. The pledge depends on the CERN Member States approving the FCC, with a decision expected around 2028.

CERN built 'Fusillo', a curved canted-cosine-theta (CCCT) superconducting dipole prototype designed to give 3 T at only 300 A. It is expected to be easier to cool by dry cooling without liquid helium. Full-scale tests were planned for April 2025, and its first use is foreseen in a new HIE-ISOLDE storage ring within about five years. Later versions could make hadron therapy more compact and affordable; CERN notes there is no hadron-therapy centre in Africa and only one under construction in South America.

On 10 Sep 2025 CERN and Fusion for Energy (F4E, the EU body managing Europe's contribution to ITER) signed a framework collaboration agreement covering high-temperature-superconductor magnets, RF power couplers and materials testing. It builds on cooperation since 2014 and on CERN's fusion-technology coordination unit set up in 2023.

GaToroid is CERN's toroidal superconducting gantry for hadron therapy. It delivers beams from many angles without rotating heavy magnets and would weigh about 12 tonnes (proton version, 5 m diameter), against up to 270 tonnes for conventional gantries. A one-third-scale demonstrator matched the predicted field to within 1%.

On 14 Oct 2025 a consortium of UNIGE, CERN, HEPIA, ID Quantique, Rolex and the Canton of Geneva launched the Geneva Quantum Network on 262 km of existing fibre. It is Switzerland's first quantum network: it distributes entangled photons between UNIGE, CERN and HEPIA, runs ID Quantique QKD, and shares time from CERN's White Rabbit system and Rolex's optical rubidium atomic clock.

In its second industrial pilot run (Nov–Dec 2025), CERN's HEARTS facility for very-high-energy heavy-ion testing of electronics hosted 16 companies and institutes for more than 200 irradiation hours. Users included a Belgian satellite-computer start-up testing SSDs and an Italian firm testing PCBs for a satellite to asteroid Apophis (2029). Six users paid for beam time.
In May 2026 CERN released its full KiCad electronics component library, more than 17,000 components with schematic symbols and PCB footprints, under an open-source licence.

In 2025 the CERN Council approved MEDICIS to supply mass-separated radionuclides for clinical treatment. In the last quarter of 2025 MEDICIS shipped actinium-225 to a private company for the first time, RayzeBio, which was then the only pharma company running phase-3 trials with Ac-225. Test deliveries to Heidelberg University Hospital followed at the end of 2025.

At the Medipix3 Collaboration's 20th-anniversary symposium (23 Sep 2025), CERN reported that Medipix4 is 'the most advanced high-resolution photon counting chip in the world'. Malvern Panalytical has been a licensee for more than 25 years, and MARS Bioimaging's 3D colour X-ray scanner entered clinical trials at the Hospital for Special Surgery, New York, in 2025.

The EU PRISMAP programme, coordinated by CERN-MEDICIS, finished on 31 Dec 2025 after 5 years. It delivered 159 batches of 23 different radionuclides to 47 medical research projects in 19 countries, linking 8 production facilities and 5 biomedical centres. Among them was a Pb-203/Pb-212 'theranostic pair' for prostate-cancer research in Dresden.

RayzeBio, MEDICIS's first industrial Ac-225 customer, was bought by Bristol Myers Squibb for about USD 4.1 billion ($62.50 per share in cash). The deal closed on 26 Feb 2024, and RayzeBio's lead drug RYZ101 (225Ac-DOTATATE) was in a phase-3 trial.

CERN's ROOT data-analysis software was adapted, in the HighLO project with CORMEC and Wageningen University, to detect market manipulation in high-frequency trading data. Trading venues such as Deutsche Börse have used the tools for market surveillance, and the software is supporting ongoing market-manipulation litigation in Germany.

Former CERN engineer and ESA astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski flew Axiom-4 (25 Jun–15 Jul 2025, 20 days). On the ISS he operated SpaceRadMon-NG, a miniature radiation monitor based on LHC radiation-monitoring technology, developed in 2024 by CERN with the Polish start-up SigmaLabs (founded by CERN alumni).

About 100 CERN-linked start-ups are tracked (founded by alumni, using CERN technology or otherwise linked), plus ~60 more self-reported. Per Crunchbase, 27 of them closed 111 investment deals from 2008 to 2025, totalling CHF 3.2 billion (USD 3.8 billion in the full study). The total is dominated by a single ~USD 2.5 billion (≈CHF 2.4 billion per home.cern) post-IPO debt raise by Novartis in 2024, counted under Advanced Accelerator Applications, a CERN spin-off Novartis bought in 2017 for USD 3.9 billion. Without it, the other companies raised roughly USD 1.3 billion.

A Technopolis/CSIL study of CERN's socio-economic benefits (carried out Feb–Dec 2025, published June 2026) found that firms that won their first CERN order between 2016 and 2024 had, within five years and compared with a control group, +15% patent stock, +63% intangible assets, +14% turnover, +13% employment and +27% tangible assets. 54% of suppliers surveyed in 2024 entered new markets because of their work with CERN.

In July 2025 CERN and the International Cancer Expert Corps hosted a STELLA progress meeting at CERN. STELLA aims to re-engineer radiotherapy linacs to work reliably in low- and middle-income countries, backed by a USD 1.75M US DOE grant (May 2024), Oxford, Cambridge and Lancaster, and a network of 28 LMICs. In Africa there is about 1 radiotherapy machine per 3.5 million people, against 1 per 80,000–100,000 in the US and Europe.

CERN and the Irish company SuperNode built a vacuum-compatibility test rig for a novel cryostat for superconducting cables, en route to SuperNode's cryogenic centre in Dublin as of 1 Sep 2025. Replacing stainless-steel corrugated sheaths with polymer-based materials cuts losses and increases the distance between cooling stations more than fivefold. Ireland became a CERN Associate Member State on 22 Oct 2025 (agreement signed May 2025), and the Irish government highlighted SuperNode as a case study in its membership announcement (SuperNode news, 13 Nov 2025).

CERN's CAFEIN federated-learning platform underpins UMBRELLA, a 5-year EU Innovative Health Initiative project launched in Oct 2024 with more than 20 public and private partners. It trains AI for stroke diagnosis and prognosis across hospitals without moving patient data. Europe has more than 1 million acute strokes a year and nearly 10 million stroke survivors.

CERN's Quantum Technology Initiative opened a quantum-network lab (Sep 2025), with Single Quantum (superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors) and Qunnect (entangled-photon sources) contributing in kind. It sent the White Rabbit timing signal and entangled photons through the same optical fibre for the first time at CERN, at sub-nanosecond accuracy and picosecond-level synchronisation.

LHCb measured Δms = 17.7656 ± 0.0057 ps^-1 (legacy combination, Nature Physics 2022). That corresponds to about 2.8 trillion full particle→antiparticle→particle cycles per second (Δms/2π). In its mean lifetime of about 1.5 ps a Bs0 completes about 4 full cycles, which means it changes identity about 9 times.

On 1 August 2026, at ICHEP 2026 in Natal, Brazil, LHCb reported a new beauty-strange meson, Bs0*(5700)0, seen in the Bs0π0 mass spectrum at more than 7σ. Its mass is 5698.9 ± 1.5 ± 0.6 ± 0.1 MeV/c² and its width is below 9.8 MeV (90% CL). It is lighter and narrower than the quark model predicts, and could be the long-sought chiral partner of the Bs0 or the first exotic hadron with a single bottom quark.

The ultra-rare decay Bs0 → μ+μ−, which the Standard Model predicts for about 4 in every billion Bs0 mesons, was first observed in a combined CMS+LHCb analysis published in Nature in 2015 (more than 6σ). LHCb alone observed it at 7.8σ in 2017, and its 2022 measurement gives a branching fraction of about 3.09×10^-9, in line with the Standard Model.

As of 29 April 2025 the LHCb collaboration had 1784 members from 102 institutes in 24 countries, and 1204 authors, which made it the third-largest experimental collaboration at CERN. By then LHCb had produced 769 physics papers, not counting performance papers.

In June 2026 LHCb said the collaboration 'is on the verge of exceeding 2000 members (approximately double its size of 15 years ago)'. On 1 July 2026 Tim Gershon (Warwick) became spokesperson and Paula Collins (CERN) deputy spokesperson, succeeding Vincenzo Vagnoni's team.
On 1 December 2025 LHCb had 1844 members from 108 institutes in 27 countries plus CERN, about 68 new members a year on average, and 811 physics papers.

claim_en: LHCb made the first observation of CP violation in baryons, the type of particle ordinary matter is built from. Using more than 80,000 Λb0 → p K− π+ π− decays, it measured a CP asymmetry ACP = (2.45 ± 0.46 ± 0.10)%, 5.2σ from zero. The result was announced at Moriond on 25 March 2025 and published in Nature on 16 July 2025 (vol. 643, pp. 1223–1228).

On 21 March 2019 LHCb made the first observation of CP violation in charm particles, measuring ΔACP = (−0.154 ± 0.029)% at 5.3σ from tens of millions of D0 decays recorded in 2011–2018. Charm had been discovered in 1974. Makoto Kobayashi (Nobel 2008) commented: 'I hope that analysis of the results will provide a clue to new physics.'
Since 2010 LHCb has collected more than 100 PB of data; after the 2019-2022 upgrade it records tens of PB a year, with another 60 PB expected before Run 3 ended in 2026 (March 2025 abstract).
When the full Run 1 dataset was released (20 December 2023), LHCb data from Runs 1 and 2 had been used for over 700 scientific publications.
quote: LHCb data across runs I and II have been used for over 700 scientific publications including a number of significant discoveries.

claim_en: In 2024 alone LHCb recorded 9.56 fb^-1 of 13.6 TeV proton–proton data, more than Run 1 and Run 2 combined (9 fb^-1). LHCb reports 11.8 fb^-1 of high-quality pp data in 2025 and 5.34 fb^-1 in 2026. In spring 2026 a single LHC fill of almost 50 hours gave LHCb a record 366 pb^-1, more than the whole 2015 data-taking year.

The LHCb detector weighs 5600 tonnes, is 21 m long, 10 m high and 13 m wide, and sits 100 m underground near Ferney-Voltaire, France. It is a forward spectrometer: its subdetectors stand one behind another over about 20 m and record particles thrown forward on one side of the collision.

LHCb has discovered all three doubly charmed baryons. Ξcc++ (ccu) came in 2017. Ξcc+ (ccd) was announced on 17 March 2026 at Moriond at more than 7σ, with m = 3619.97 ± 0.83 ± 0.26 (+1.90/−1.30) MeV/c², about 3.9 times the proton mass, from about 915 candidates in 2024 data. It was the first new particle found with the upgraded detector, and it resolved the unconfirmed 2002 SELEX (Fermilab) claim of a much lighter state. Ωcc+ (ccs) was announced on 3 June 2026 at Beauty 2026 in Maastricht ('mass peak ... around 3727 MeV/c²'). The paper (arXiv:2609.21921, 18 Sep 2026) reports 8.7σ and m = 3725.9 ± 1.0 ± 0.2 ± 0.4 ± 0.6 MeV/c² from 6.3 fb^-1 at 13.6 TeV (2024). This completes the ground-state spin-1/2 doubly charmed family, 'predicted to exist for over 50 years'.
LHCb's 2024 average event sizes before and after Sprucing: FULL 114.9 to 33.8 kB, TURBO 13.4 to 10.2 kB, TURCAL 176.9 to 21.2 kB, so a stored event is roughly 10-100 kB.

At the end of April 2026 the LHC ran briefly at 1.2 TeV per beam instead of 6.8 TeV. LHCb used its SMOG2 gas cell in front of the VELO to inject hydrogen, deuterium, helium, neon, argon and xenon and recorded more than one billion events per gas. These measurements help interpret cosmic-ray antimatter measured by space experiments such as AMS (on the ISS) and PAMELA. With this run, LHCb's Run 3 reached 25 different collision systems.

Patrick Koppenburg's (LHCb) list of new particles discovered at the LHC states 'So far 86 hadrons have been discovered at the LHC, of which 76 by LHCb'. The latest entry is the Bs0*(5700)0, dated 21 Sep 2026. Only first observations above 5σ are counted.

In Run 3 LHCb's first software trigger stage (HLT1) runs at the average non-empty bunch-crossing rate of 30 MHz, the readout handles the 40 MHz crossing rate, and the Run 1-2 hardware trigger was limited to 1 MHz.

In March 2021 LHCb measured the lepton-universality ratio R(K) 3.1σ below the Standard Model prediction. On 20 December 2022 a new analysis of the full Run 1 + Run 2 data found R(K) and R(K*) compatible with the Standard Model within 1σ, and it supersedes the earlier results. Spokesperson Chris Parkes explained that the difference came mainly from an improved understanding of hadrons misidentified as electrons, a background that had been underestimated before.

Lithuania has been a CERN Associate Member State since 2018 and pays about €1 million a year; full membership would cost about €4 million a year. According to LRT, Lithuania sent an official letter to CERN at the end of August 2026 seeking full membership, and CERN's head of research and computing, Gautier Hamel de Monchenault, said 'The membership procedure has already started.'

LHCb specialises in the small differences between matter and antimatter, studied mainly through particles containing the beauty (b) quark, to understand why the Universe seems to be made almost entirely of matter and almost no antimatter.

A small LHCb simulated sample released in 2020 was used externally for a paper on quantum-inspired machine learning (arXiv:2004.13747); several of its authors are LHCb members, so 'external' is the proceedings' wording.

On 5 July 2022 LHCb announced three new exotic particles: the first pentaquark containing a strange quark (15σ) and the first-ever pair of tetraquarks, one doubly charged (6.5σ) and one neutral (8σ). Physics coordinator Niels Tuning said: 'We're creating particle zoo 2.0'.

On 14 July 2015 LHCb reported the observation of pentaquark states, Pc(4450)+ and Pc(4380)+. They are made of two up quarks, one down quark, one charm quark and one charm antiquark, and were seen in Λb → J/ψ p K− decays. They were the first convincing pentaquarks after more than 50 years of searches since Gell-Mann's 1964 quark model.

In March 2019, with a Λb sample nine times larger than in 2015, LHCb discovered a new narrow pentaquark, Pc(4312)+, at 7.3σ. It also showed that the 2015 Pc(4450)+ is actually two narrow peaks, Pc(4440)+ and Pc(4457)+ (5.4σ over a single peak). The narrow states support the idea that they may be loosely bound baryon–meson 'molecules'.

LHCb does 'real-time analysis': the trigger performs offline-quality reconstruction, alignment and calibration, so most selected events are stored only as the reconstructed physics objects ('Turbo' format) instead of raw detector data. CERN's March 2023 article says this lets LHCb 'not only cherry-pick interesting events but also compress the raw detector data in real time'. In the design, 68% of triggered events are Turbo.
LHCb's latest incremental re-Stripping of Run 1 read 2.5 PB and wrote 350 TB; a 2023-2024 campaign on 6.17 PB of 2016-2018 data produced 1.48 PB.

Vilnius University: Dr Šarpis was responsible for preparing the Run 1 (2011-2012) data set and for the technical implementation of LHCb's Open Data Release; the article compares Run 1 to 250 million photos or 35 years of HD video.

LHC Run 3 ended on 27 June 2026, when protons last circulated; the last pp collisions were on 16 May 2026 and the last lead–lead collisions on 14 June 2026. The LHC has now delivered nearly 550 fb^-1 since 2009 and has entered Long Shutdown 3, a four-year upgrade to the High-Luminosity LHC. LHCb says it is entering 'a four-year shutdown before Run 4'.

The upgraded LHCb detector processes an average of 4 TB/s in real time in Run 3, reading out the full detector for every bunch crossing. Source: arXiv:2106.07701, 'Evolution of the energy efficiency of LHCb's real-time processing', EPJ Web Conf. 251 (2021) 04009; Allen is a different paper, arXiv:1912.09161.

claim_en: The new LHCb Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) tracker is built from more than 11,000 km of 250 µm-diameter plastic scintillating fibre. After zero suppression it sends about 20 Tbit/s to the data acquisition over 4096 links.

LHCb's first observation of Λb⁰ → Σc⁽*⁾⁺⁺D⁽*⁾⁻K⁻ decays (Run 2, 6 fb⁻¹; PRD 110 (2024) L031104) found four modes, Σc⁺⁺D⁻K⁻ with 480 ± 25 candidates at 32σ; with O(100) candidates per mode it is too small for an amplitude analysis.
In Run 3 LHCb's design data rate to tape is 10 GB/s, and Sprucing reduces it to 3.5 GB/s for disk; in 2024 Analysis Productions processed 14 PB of data in a single day.

In 2021 LHCb discovered the Tcc+, a tetraquark with two charm quarks and an anti-up and anti-down quark (cc ū d̄). It was seen at well above 20σ, and its mass lies a fraction of an MeV below the D0 D*+ threshold. CERN's EP newsletter calls it the longest-lived exotic hadron yet, with a lifetime 10–1000 times longer than other exotic particles, 'a whisker away from stability'.

In Run 3 LHCb reads the whole detector out at 30 MHz into its software trigger, about 40 Tbit/s (5 TB/s), and writes about 10 GB/s to storage: about one byte kept in 500. After the first stage the data wait in a ~30 PB disk buffer, so the final decision comes hours to days later, not instantly; on average 5 proton collisions happen per crossing.

claim_en: For Run 3 (from 2022) LHCb removed its hardware trigger. The detector was almost completely renewed to run at an instantaneous luminosity five times higher (2×10^33 cm^-2 s^-1). Every non-empty bunch crossing (30 MHz) is read out into an all-software trigger: about 4 TB/s of data is reduced in real time to about 10 GB/s written to storage, a factor of about 400.

On 14 April 2025 LHCb announced that the LHC Committee had concluded its review of the Upgrade II Scoping Document and that the CERN Research Board had endorsed its conclusions, recommending the 'Middle' scenario. The planned timeline: subdetector TDRs in 2026, construction done by mid-2032, installation in LS4 (2034–35), data-taking from Run 5 in 2036, aiming at 300 fb^-1 with fast-timing, radiation-hard detectors.

In early 2026 UKRI cancelled the remaining UK funding for LHCb Upgrade II. STFC had awarded £49.4 million in 2022, and about £5 million had been spent. The whole upgrade is estimated at about £150 million. STFC's prioritisation outcomes for 2026–2030 (published 9 July 2026) list 'LHCb Upgrade 2: Not prioritised for further funding'. Tim Gershon: 'It's like paying to heat your house but then sitting outside in the cold.'

In the upgraded LHCb Vertex Locator (VELO, from 2022) the edge of the closest active silicon pixel is 5.1 mm from the beam line, down from 8.2 mm in the original VELO. The RF box separating detector vacuum from the LHC beam vacuum has an inner radius of only 3.5 mm. The two VELO halves are retracted by 29 mm except during stable beams.

In January 2023, during a warm-up of the VELO, equipment failed and the pumps built up a differential pressure about 10 times above specification. This plastically deformed the thin RF boxes facing the beam. The sensor modules were not damaged, but in 2023 the VELO could not be fully closed, so that year's data were of reduced quality. The RF boxes were completely replaced in the 2023–24 shutdown.

The upgraded VELO has 52 modules with about 41 million 55 µm × 55 µm pixels (the old one had 172 thousand strip channels). It reads out zero-suppressed at 40 MHz, produces about 2 Tbit/s (peak up to 2.85 Tbit/s) and dissipates about 2 kW in vacuum. It is cooled by evaporative CO2 flowing through microchannels etched in silicon.

VeloPix is based on Timepix3, developed by the Medipix/Timepix collaborations at CERN. The hybrid-pixel technology was originally developed for particle physics, went into medical X-ray imaging (Medipix) and came back to HEP. The CERN Medipix page calls VeloPix 'a direct spin back to high-energy physics'. VeloPix is made in TSMC 130 nm CMOS, has 256×256 pixels of 55 µm and handles up to 900 million hits/s, against 80 million for Timepix3. It is radiation hard to more than 4 MGy.
